lines.text: A force can pull diagonally, while equilibrium equations are easiest along chosen axes. Its horizontal and vertical effects must be kept with their directions.

Forces are vectors, they have magnitude and direction. Resolving a force replaces it by components whose vector sum is the original force. If a force P is at angle theta above the positive horizontal, its horizontal component is P cosine theta right and its vertical component is P sine theta up. The cosine component is adjacent to the stated angle. For forces directed left or down, give that component a negative sign on right or up positive axes. Coplanar forces can be resolved along any convenient pair of perpendicular axes, on a slope, axes parallel and perpendicular to the plane simplify the equations.
This uses vector components from earlier mechanics. The same resolution turns the vector equilibrium condition into two scalar equations.

Draw the force arrow and mark the angle it makes with an axis. Resolve into perpendicular components, assign each a direction and sign. At angle theta above horizontal, P x equals P cosine theta, P y equals P sine theta.
A force points thirty degrees above the horizontal. Which component is adjacent to that angle, and how do you know?

A force P points thirty degrees above the horizontal. Which is its horizontal component? P cosine thirty degrees right P sine thirty degrees right P right P cosine thirty degrees up ay The horizontal component is adjacent to the given angle and points right.
A stationary particle can still have several substantial forces on it. Their combined effect, rather than each individual force, determines equilibrium.

For equilibrium under coplanar forces, the vector resultant is zero. Resolve all forces on the particle along two perpendicular axes and set both component sums to zero. Weight m g acts vertically downward, with g equals nine point eight metres per second squared. A normal reaction acts perpendicular to a contact surface. Tension pulls along a taut string, thrust pushes along a strut or contact direction. Friction acts along a rough contact and opposes the actual or impending relative motion. On a plane inclined at theta to the horizontal, weight has component m g sine theta down the plane and m g cosine theta into it. For a smooth plane held by a string parallel to the plane, equilibrium gives T equals m g sine theta and R equals m g cosine theta. Include any other forces before using those special case equations.
The free body diagram used in Newton's laws also works here, equilibrium is the case with zero acceleration and zero resultant.

Isolate one particle and draw weight, normal reaction, tension or thrust, and friction as appropriate. Choose two perpendicular axes and use the sum of F x equals zero, the sum of F y equals zero. On an incline, resolve weight as m g sine theta along and m g cosine theta normal to the plane.
Why can several nonzero forces act on a particle that remains in equilibrium?

A particle rests on a smooth slope, held by a string parallel to the slope. Which force balances the downslope weight component? The normal reaction The string tension Friction The total weight B The string tension acts up the slope, opposite the m g sine theta component.
A rough surface can hold a particle still under a range of applied pulls. The friction force changes with the pull until the limiting value is reached.

The coefficient of friction mu relates the greatest available friction to the normal reaction R. For a particle in equilibrium, the actual friction magnitude F satisfies F is less than or equal to mu R. First use the force balance to find the F required to prevent motion. Then find R from the perpendicular balance and check the inequality. Friction acts opposite the impending relative motion, not necessarily opposite the positive axis. At limiting equilibrium the particle is just about to slip, so F equals mu R. For a rough horizontal surface with only weight and reaction vertically, R equals m g, the largest horizontal pull that can be balanced is mu m g. If the required friction exceeds mu R, the particle cannot remain in equilibrium.
This extends the equilibrium equations with a bound on one force. The equality rule is the threshold case of the inequality.

In equilibrium, actual friction obeys F is less than or equal to mu R. Find R by resolving perpendicular to contact, then find F needed for balance. At limiting equilibrium only, use F equals mu R, friction opposes impending relative motion.
Why can friction be smaller than mu R even when the particle is at rest?

A particle remains at rest while a small horizontal pull is applied. What sets the actual friction magnitude? It is always mu R It equals the pull needed for horizontal balance, provided it does not exceed mu R It is always zero It equals the normal reaction B Static friction adjusts to the value needed for equilibrium, up to its limiting value mu R.

five Statics of a particle.
In one breath.

A particle is in equilibrium when the vector sum of all forces acting on it is zero. Resolve forces along two perpendicular axes, then use the two zero sum equations, for static friction, use F is less than or equal to mu R.
Key ideas.

A force as a vector has a magnitude and a direction. To resolve a force means to replace it with components whose vector sum is the original force. If a force P acts at angle theta above the horizontal, its rightward component is P cosine theta and its upward component is P sine theta. State the axes and directions before using signs. For a downward force or a force pointing left, the corresponding signed component is negative.

A particle in equilibrium has zero resultant force. For coplanar forces, resolving in any two perpendicular directions gives the sum of F x equals zero and the sum of F y equals zero. These two equations must both hold. Equilibrium does not mean that each force is zero, nonzero forces balance one another.

Weight is m g vertically downward, using g equals nine point eight metres per second squared. A normal reaction R acts perpendicular to a contact surface. Tension pulls along a taut string, thrust pushes along a strut or contact direction. Friction lies along the contact surface and opposes actual or impending relative motion. On a horizontal surface without another vertical force, R equals m g. If an upward pull has a vertical component, that component reduces R. On a slope, resolve the weight along and perpendicular to the plane, the components are m g sine theta down the plane and m g cosine theta into the plane.

The coefficient of friction mu sets the maximum available static friction. In equilibrium, F is less than or equal to mu R. The actual friction F is what the force balance requires. At limiting equilibrium, the particle is just about to slip, so F equals mu R. If the force needed for balance exceeds mu R, equilibrium is impossible.
Method.
Isolate the particle. Draw every force acting on it, with its direction, weight, reaction, tension or thrust, applied forces and friction where appropriate.
Choose convenient perpendicular axes. On a slope, take one axis along the plane and one normal to it. Resolve angled forces with sine and cosine relative to the stated angle.
Write a zero resultant equation on each axis. Solve these equations for the unknown forces.

For rough contact, first find R, then find the friction needed for equilibrium. Check F is less than or equal to mu R, use equality only when the question says the particle is on the point of moving or asks for a maximum or minimum threshold.
Worked example.

A three kilograms particle rests on a smooth plane inclined at thirty degrees, held by a string parallel to the plane. Find the tension and reaction. Along the plane, T minus three g sine thirty degrees equals zero, so T equals fourteen point seven newtons. Perpendicular to the plane, R minus three g cosine thirty degrees equals zero, so R is approximately twenty five point five newtons to three significant figures. Check the directions, tension acts uphill, reaction acts out of the plane. Their components balance weight, so the resultant is zero.
Traps.

Trap, Using sine theta for every horizontal component. Why it's wrong, the angle may be measured from the horizontal, making the horizontal component adjacent. Instead, draw the component triangle and label the given angle.
Trap, Writing R equals m g automatically. Why it's wrong, contact angle and other vertical forces change the perpendicular balance. Instead, resolve normal to the surface.
Trap, Writing F equals mu R whenever a particle rests. Why it's wrong, static friction may be smaller than its maximum. Instead, find the required F from equilibrium, then check the inequality.
Exam technique.

For Calculate and Find, show the force equations before substituting numbers. For Explain, state why friction points in its chosen direction and why equality with mu R does or does not apply. Give numerical answers to two or three significant figures after using g equals nine point eight.
